newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: Sorrell sees big shake-up in advertising industry.
newsitem.headline: Sorrell sees big shake-up in advertising industry.

text.p: Global advertising agencies, recently hit by tumultuous changes in ownership, must brace themselves for more big shake-ups, the head of the world's largest advertising and marketing services group said on Friday.

Martin Sorrell, group chief executive of WPP Group Plc, told a business conference to expect an increasing polarisation of big and small agencies, with medium-sized agencies getting swallowed up or pushed aside.
"I see an almost unprecedented period of instability in advertising agency ownership," he said in Amsterdam.
"...I think that heralds a major consolidation of the industry," he said at the closing of the two-day annual European conference of the International Advertising Association (IAA).
He cited advertising holding companies like Cordiant Plc in Britain, True North Communications Inc in the United States and Publicis and Havas in France.
London-based Cordiant, which owns Saatchi & Saatchi Advertising and Bates Worldwide, announced in April it would demerge the two ad agencies by setting them up as separate listed companies.
In February True North, the parent of Foote, Cone & Belding, the largest advertising agency in North America, and Paris-based Publicis agreed to end their global partnership.
Havas, the French communications group, has been looking at cutting its 37-percent stake in Havas Advertising.
Sorrell also mentioned turmoil and change at Leo Burnett and Young & Rubicam advertising agencies in the United States.
In March Leo Burnett announced the resignation of its top two executives and late last year Young & Rubicam sold a 20-percent stake in the agency to Hellman & Friedman, a U.S. investment firm.
Sorrell had a few comforting words for ad agencies shaken up in recent years by clients' insistence on replacing old fixed-commission payments with new flexible fees.

Many clients have insisted on paying with fees to make agencies more accountable for time and effort spent on creating ads and have switched away from a traditional commission that represented 15 percent of the money clients spent on buying media advertising space.

Sorrell said about half of WPP's 40-odd companies were ad agencies or others companies used to getting paid by commission. He said about 70 percent of those still got paid by commission, while 30 percent now got paid by clients with fees.
Sorrell said the other half of WPP's companies got paid on a fee basis and had always used that system.

"There's been a big switch from commissions to fees...But the situation has stablised..." he told the IAA, which groups ad agencies and other marketing companies, media owners and advertisers, the companies that spent money on advertising.
Sorrell said too many ad agencies had "pooh-poohed" the importance of the Internet and other new media.

He suggested younger people might soon climb the ranks in ad agencies, since most agencies were run by 40- to 50-year-olds who failed to understand the importance, power and -- for children as young as four years old -- the accessibility of the computer world.
"It's a generational thing -- and I think you're going to see that change," he said.
WPP has made a total of about $15 million in investments in six new media-related companies, he said.
